title: Critical Thinking (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Common core of 17 conceptions: critical thinking = 'careful goal-directed thinking'; Dewey called it reflective thinking ('active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief').

Abilities listed include observing, questioning (turning puzzlement into a clear question), inferring, testing hypotheses, consulting and judging source credibility, argument analysis, and imagining alternative explanations.
Dispositions: attentiveness, habit of inquiry, open-mindedness, willingness to suspend judgment, seeking the truth; subject knowledge is also required.
Reports Abrami et al. 2015: dialogue, anchored instruction and mentoring help, combination best; evidence that instruction transfers across domains is described as scanty.
practical_applications: Use the ability list as the skeleton of the pre-delivery check (question, evidence, source credibility, alternatives).
Do not assume a generic 'think critically' instruction transfers; use domain-specific checklists.
limitations: Philosophical overview, not an empirical review; the last ~13% of the page text was not read.
Author not shown in the text read; first published 2018-07-21, last substantive revision 2022-10-12.

title: Fallacies (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: A fallacy can be treated as an argument that seems better than it really is; academic writers favour this 'deceptively bad argument' view over 'false popular belief'.
Discusses textbook tradition (Copi's 18 informal fallacies) incl. equivocation, composition/division, begging the question, complex question.
practical_applications: Check our own captions/scripts for arguments that only look strong (e.g., one testimonial presented as proof).
limitations: Only a search summary was read; archived editions 2016-2025 exist, original year not captured.

title: Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Abrami, P. C.; Bernard, R. M.; Borokhovski, E.; Waddington, D. I.; Wade, C. A.; Persson, T.
key_findings: 341 effect sizes, weighted mean g = 0.30 (range about -1 to +2), learners from elementary to adult (per SEP supplement and Clearinghouse commentary).
Dialogue, anchored (authentic problem) instruction and mentoring each helped; combinations worked best (per SEP).
practical_applications: Critical thinking is trainable but effects are small-moderate; build it into routines (checklists, dialogue/critique) rather than relying on intention.
limitations: Read via secondary summaries; most studies lack long-term follow-up.

title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
key_findings: Three heuristics: representativeness, availability, adjustment from an anchor; economical and usually effective but lead to systematic and predictable errors.
Representativeness ignores factors such as base rates and sample size that should affect probability.
practical_applications: When judging 'which idea will work', ask for base rates (how did similar posts perform?) instead of how vivid/typical the idea feels.
limitations: Abstract and excerpts only; classic lab vignettes.

title: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises
key_findings: Confirmation bias = seeking or interpreting evidence in ways partial to existing beliefs; review states a great deal of empirical evidence shows it is extensive, strong and appears in many guises.
practical_applications: Before delivery, actively look for evidence against the chosen claim/idea, not just support.
limitations: Only abstract and opening pages read; narrative review, not meta-analysis.

title: Considering the opposite: A corrective strategy for social judgment
authors: Lord, C. G.; Lepper, M. R.; Preston, E.
key_findings: Two experiments (biased assimilation of evidence; biased hypothesis testing): inducing a 'consider the opposite' strategy corrected bias more than instructions to be 'as fair and unbiased as possible'.
practical_applications: Pre-delivery item: write the strongest case that the opposite is true; 'be objective' instructions are weaker.
limitations: Abstract only; 1980s student samples; no large modern replication found this session.

title: Giving Debiasing Away: Can Psychological Research on Correcting Cognitive Errors Promote Human Welfare?
authors: Lilienfeld, S. O.; Ammirati, R.; Landfield, K.
key_findings: Reviews what is known and unknown about debiasing confirmation bias and barriers to real-world effectiveness; research cataloguing biases far outweighs research on debiasing.
practical_applications: Treat any debiasing step as uncertain; prefer structural safeguards (checklists, second reviewer) over self-exhortation.
limitations: Abstract/introduction only; specific technique evidence not read.

title: Debiasing Decisions: Improved Decision Making With a Single Training Intervention
authors: Morewedge, C. K.; Yoon, H.; Scopelliti, I.; Symborski, C. W.; Korris, J. H.; Kassam, K. S.
key_findings: Two longitudinal experiments: one-shot training (video game or instructional video) produced medium to large debiasing effects immediately, persisting at least 2 months.
Games with personalized feedback and practice beat videos; effects were domain-general across taught and untaught formats.
practical_applications: Practice with feedback beats reading about biases: log our own wrong calls in LEARNING-LOG and review them.
limitations: Abstract only (full text blocked); games cost ~USD 7M to build (BU note); biases targeted were those relevant to intelligence analysis.
Published in Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences 2(1):129-140; DOI not captured this session.

title: Debiasing Training Improves Decision Making in the Field
authors: Sellier, A.-L.; Scopelliti, I.; Morewedge, C. K.
key_findings: Field experiment, 290 French business graduate students; one-shot confirmation-bias game before an unannounced Challenger-style business case.
Trained students were 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming option; write-ups suggest less confirmatory hypothesis testing.
practical_applications: Evidence that debiasing can transfer to a realistic case; supports building a habit of testing the rival hypothesis.
limitations: Single field experiment by the authors' own account; one population; abstract/summary only.

title: The Trouble With Overconfidence
authors: Moore, D. A.; Healy, P. J.
key_findings: Overconfidence is three distinct constructs: overestimation (own performance), overplacement (vs others), overprecision (excess certainty).
Hard tasks produce overestimation and underplacement; easy tasks the reverse; overprecision is the most persistent (later summary).
practical_applications: State uncertainty ranges and confidence labels rather than single confident claims (targets overprecision).
limitations: Abstract and secondary summaries only.

title: Investigating Variation in Replicability: A 'Many Labs' Replication Project
authors: Klein, R. A.; Ratliff, K. A.; Vianello, M.; et al.
key_findings: 13 effects, 36 samples, 6,344 participants; 10 replicated consistently; flag priming and currency priming did not; imagined contact weak.
Replicability depended more on the effect than on sample/setting.
Effects tested included anchoring, gain-vs-loss framing, sunk costs, retrospective gambler's fallacy; Nature coverage says anchoring was substantially stronger than the original study suggested.
practical_applications: Classic judgment effects (anchoring, framing) are among the more robust; subtle priming claims are not - do not build content on them.
limitations: Full text blocked (403); per-effect outcome for framing/sunk cost not confirmed this session.

title: Timid Choices and Bold Forecasts: A Cognitive Perspective on Risk Taking
key_findings: Decision makers treat problems as unique; overly optimistic forecasts come from an 'inside view' anchored on specific plans and scenarios; the 'outside view' (later: reference-class forecasting) uses outcomes of similar past cases.
practical_applications: Estimate time/performance of a new clip from how similar past clips actually went (our render logs, past reach), not from the plan.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament
authors: Mellers, B.; Ungar, L.; Baron, J.; et al.
key_findings: In the IARPA tournament, probability training (correcting biases, using reference classes, averaging estimates), teaming and tracking each improved calibration and resolution.
practical_applications: Probabilistic language ('likely ~70%') plus reference classes is trainable and improves judgment.
limitations: Abstract only; geopolitical forecasting domain.

title: Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events
authors: Mitchell, D. J.; Russo, J. E.; Pennington, N.
key_findings: Secondary sources (premortem write-ups) report that imagining an event as having already happened ('prospective hindsight') increased the number of reasons generated by about 30%.
practical_applications: Basis for the pre-mortem item: 'it is next week and this post flopped/misled people - why?'.
limitations: Existence confirmed (J. Behavioral Decision Making 2(1):25-38); content not read; the 30% figure is from secondary sources only.

title: Performing a Project Premortem
key_findings: HBR 85(9):18-19. Team assumes the project has failed and each member lists plausible reasons; held at the start so the plan can be fixed; claimed to prime people to notice early warning signs.
practical_applications: 2-minute pre-mortem before shipping a clip or a factual carousel.
limitations: Practitioner article; read via secondary summaries; effectiveness claims rest on small studies (Veinott2010, Mitchell1989).

title: Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence
authors: Veinott, E. S.; Klein, G.; Wiggins, S.
key_findings: Secondary accounts: 178 students evaluating an H1N1 response plan; premortem reduced (over)confidence more than simple critique or pros-and-cons.
practical_applications: Premortem is a reasonable cheap tool to lower overconfidence in a plan.
limitations: Conference proceedings (ISCRAM); measured confidence, not real-world plan failure; content known only via secondary sources.

title: The problem with '5 whys'
key_findings: 5 Whys has value as a teaching tool ('aha' of systems safety) but is weak for root cause analysis: oversimplifies complex problems, the number five is arbitrary, no objective stopping rule, tends toward a single causal chain.
practical_applications: Use 5 Whys only for quick single-chain glitches (render bug); for audience/performance problems list multiple contributing causes.
limitations: Commentary in a healthcare context; read via PSNet summary and excerpts (full text 403).

title: The problem with root cause analysis
authors: Peerally, M. F.; Carr, S.; Waring, J.; Dixon-Woods, M.
key_findings: The term 'root cause' implies a single cause and promotes reductionism; RCA applied without adaptation; eight challenges incl. single-point causation focus and weak feedback.
practical_applications: When a series underperforms, record several contributing factors (hook, timing, topic, format) and test one at a time.
limitations: Healthcare context; abstract and summaries only.

title: The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?
key_findings: Nine viewpoints (strength, consistency, etc.) for judging whether an association is causal; commentators stress Hill did not call them criteria.
Core practical question: will changing A change the frequency of B?
practical_applications: Before saying 'X causes Y' (e.g., 'screens cause myopia'), check strength, consistency, dose-response and plausible alternatives; otherwise write 'linked with'.
limitations: Read via summaries (Wakeford, Milbank, ASU) not the full text.

title: Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability
key_findings: Secondary sources describe it as an accessible summary/guide to Wald's WWII memoranda on estimating aircraft survivability from returning planes (the classic survivorship-bias case).
practical_applications: When copying 'what viral posts do', remember we only see survivors; flops that did the same thing are invisible.
limitations: JASA 79(386) per a single secondary source; content not read; popular retellings embellish the story (AMS 'Legend of Abraham Wald').
